techniques.name: Brute Force
techniques.description: Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained. Without knowledge of the password for an account or set of accounts, an adversary may systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism, sometimes trying every possible combination or a curated list of likely candidates.

techniques.name: Brute Force: Password Guessing
techniques.description: Adversaries with no prior knowledge of legitimate credentials on a system or in an environment may guess passwords to attempt access to accounts. Without knowledge of the password for an account, an adversary may opt to systematically guess the password using a repetitive or iterative mechanism against one or a small number of accounts.

techniques.name: Brute Force: Password Spraying
techniques.description: Adversaries may use a single or small list of commonly used passwords against many different accounts to attempt to acquire valid account credentials. Password spraying uses one password (e.g. 'Password01'), or a small list of commonly used passwords, against many different accounts on a network, avoiding account lockouts that would normally occur when brute forcing a single account with many passwords.

techniques.name: Valid Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion. Compromised credentials may be used to bypass access controls placed on various resources on systems within a network and may even be used for persistent access to remote systems. Anomalous account usage patterns — logins from unfamiliar sources, off-hours activity, or activity inconsistent with a location a user was recently active from — are common signals that a valid account's credentials have been compromised.

techniques.name: Network Service Discovery
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation. Common methods include port and/or vulnerability scans using tools that are brought onto a system, or native network scanning tools available on a compromised host.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution. PowerShell is a powerful interactive command-line interface and scripting environment included in the Windows operating system. Common indicators of malicious use include base64-encoded commands, execution-policy bypass flags, hidden windows, and download-and-execute (cradle) patterns that fetch and run remote content in memory.

techniques.name: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using the DNS application layer protocol to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic. Commands to the remote system, and often the results of those commands, will be embedded within the protocol traffic between the client and server — encoding data into subdomain labels of queries against a domain the adversary controls, so each individual query looks like normal DNS resolution rather than an outbound connection. Common indicators include a high volume of distinct, high-entropy (random-looking) subdomains queried under one base domain in a short window, and/or an elevated NXDOMAIN rate consistent with a domain-generation algorithm cycling through candidate names.

techniques.name: Resource Hijacking
techniques.description: Adversaries may leverage the resources of co-opted systems to complete resource-intensive tasks, which may impact system and/or hosted service availability. One common purpose is to validate stolen access to cloud environments, or to mine cryptocurrency, run password crackers, or operate a botnet — activity that often shows up as a sudden, sustained spike in process, network, or authentication volume on the affected host that is unusual relative to that host's own normal behavior, rather than as any single suspicious-looking event.
